title: From a Hotel Lobby in Fort Collins to a Strip Mall in Columbus: Indian Food Is Showing Up Everywhere
excerpt: A new wave of Indian restaurants is quietly spreading into mid-sized American cities far from the coastal corridors, driven by immigrant families betting on untapped appetites.
body:
The next frontier for Indian food in America is not a Michelin-starred tasting menu in Manhattan. It is a shared dining room inside a Hilton Garden Inn in Fort Collins, Colorado — population 170,000, elevation 5,003 feet, and now home to its second location of Bawarchi Biryanis.

Across the country, a quiet expansion is underway. Indian restaurants are opening in mid-sized cities and suburbs that have never had much beyond the occasional buffet, driven by immigrant families who see opportunity where chains see risk.

## The Hotel Biryani

When Sunita Palusa decided to open a second Bawarchi Biryanis in Fort Collins, she did something unconventional: she put it inside a hotel. The new location shares space with the Hilton Garden Inn's existing Garden Grille and Bar, but unlike the hotel restaurant, Bawarchi is open to the public.

It is an unusual setup that reflects the pragmatism of many Indian restaurant entrepreneurs. Rather than signing an expensive standalone lease, the Palusas — who also run the adjacent Swagath Indian grocery store at their original College Avenue location — found a way to reach a new neighbourhood with lower overhead.

"I wanted to bring more community to the Harmony area and introduce more diners to South Indian cuisine," Sunita Palusa told the Fort Collins Coloradoan. The grand opening in late June offered 15 per cent off, and the response was immediate.

## The Franchise That Ate Texas

Meanwhile, Hashtag India — a Texas-born fast-casual chain that now has 13 locations across eight states — is pushing into the Atlanta suburbs. The brand, which opened its first Georgia outpost in Suwanee last year, is adding a second location in Sandy Springs, taking over a 5,900-square-foot space on Roswell Road expected to open later this summer.

What makes Hashtag India notable is its scale and geographic ambition. With locations in Texas, Nevada, California, Virginia, Maryland, North Carolina, and Georgia, the chain has quietly assembled the kind of national footprint that Indian restaurant brands have historically struggled to achieve. Its menu — goat dum biryani, tandoori chicken, Chicken Mandhakani Curry — is unapologetically Indian, without the "accessible" rebranding that some fast-casual concepts have adopted.

The expansion mirrors a broader trend. In Kansas City, Hashtag India recently opened its first location in the metro area, in Overland Park, further extending its reach into the heartland.

## Columbus Gets a Bombay House

In Columbus, Ohio, the Kondhare family is preparing to open Bombay House Restaurant & Bar near the Polaris shopping district, taking over a space vacated by the Winking Lizard chain. The concept is deliberately pan-Indian — reflecting cuisines from across the entire country rather than focusing on a single region. The family has hired chefs from different Indian regions, each bringing individual expertise to the menu.

"Guests can expect creative drinks made with fresh ingredients, premium spirits and house-made syrups and infusions," the family said. "Our goal is to create a complete dining experience where both the food and drinks celebrate the richness and diversity of Indian cuisine."

Among the dishes the Kondhares are most excited about: vada pav, the crispy potato fritter sandwich that is Mumbai's definitive street food, reimagined for an upscale setting. For Columbus's growing Indian community — and for adventurous local diners — it fills a gap that regional-focused restaurants have left open.

## The Family Bet in Small-Town Florida

In Hernando, Florida, a town of about 10,000 people north of Tampa, the Singh family is opening Palms of India — blending authentic Indian food with monthly Peruvian-influenced specials that reflect the family's mixed heritage.

Jeffrey Singh, whose father emigrated from India and previously ran an Italian restaurant in Philadelphia, called the venture deeply personal. "My parents immigrated to this country, and I was actually the first U.S.-born individual in my entire family," he told Business Debut. "We're trying to live out the American dream."

His uncle, chef Jagjit Singh, relocated from Philadelphia to run the kitchen. The restaurant is in a part of Florida where Indian food options have been virtually nonexistent — a calculated bet that demand will follow supply.

## Why Now?

The expansion into smaller cities is driven by converging forces. Indian immigration to the United States has surged, with Indians now the largest group of new immigrants. Tech jobs, university towns, and suburban growth have distributed Indian families far beyond the traditional coastal enclaves.

At the same time, the American palate has shifted. The popularity of dishes like butter chicken, biryani, and tikka masala — now staples at Costco and Trader Joe's — has created a baseline familiarity that reduces the risk for restaurateurs in unfamiliar markets.

For the families behind these openings, the calculus is straightforward. In a place like Fort Collins or Hernando, there is little competition but real demand — from homesick diaspora diners and increasingly from curious locals who have discovered Indian food through grocery aisles and social media, and now want the real thing.

nri_angle: For NRIs living outside traditional desi enclaves, these openings signal that Indian food is becoming accessible in the kinds of cities where finding a decent biryani once meant a two-hour drive.
